title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
abstract: Introduces speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes a sequence of tokens that a larger target model verifies in parallel, giving 2-3x wall-clock speedups while provably preserving the exact output distribution.
oneLiner: Use a small draft model to guess tokens, then verify them in parallel with the big model for exact-distribution speedups.
keyFinding: Speculative decoding achieves 2-3x faster decoding while provably producing the identical output distribution as the target model.
weakness: Requires a well-matched draft model plus extra memory; speedup collapses when draft and target distributions diverge.
implication: Because sampling quality is preserved exactly, this form of acceleration does not itself alter model behavior.
contributions: Proposes the verification-based speculative decoding framework with theoretically exact token sampling.
methods: Draft model proposes tokens; target model evaluates in parallel; token-level rejection sampling preserves the target distribution.
experiments: Evaluated on T5-XXL and GPT-2-class models against baseline autoregressive decoding, measuring latency and output quality.
results: 2-3x speedup across models with no measurable degradation in output quality.
limitations: Two-model setup costs memory; gains depend on draft-target alignment; suited to low-batch autoregressive generation.
futureDirections: Automatically learned draft models, scaling to larger batches, and applying speculative decoding to other generation tasks.
insights: Acceleration can be lossless if the same distribution is sampled, a key contrast to approximate early-exit methods.
relevance: Demonstrates lossless acceleration; early-exit fairness work must justify why its quality/fairness tradeoffs are acceptable when lossless options exist.

title: Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
abstract: Adds multiple parallel decoding heads on top of a frozen base LLM to predict several future tokens at once, combined with tree-based attention and typical-acceptance sampling to speed up decoding with no separate draft model.
oneLiner: Add parallel prediction heads to the base model so several tokens are guessed and verified in one step.
keyFinding: Medusa delivers 2.2x decoding speedup on Vicuna-7B/33B and 2.3x on MT-Bench while preserving generation quality, and needs no extra draft model.
weakness: Requires a training/alignment stage to learn the heads; achievable speedup is bounded by acceptance rates.
implication: A model can predict its own future tokens with aux heads, avoiding the extra-draft-model cost of prior schemes.
contributions: Multiple prediction heads, tree-based attention for parallel verification, and typical-acceptance sampling to correct rejection bias.
methods: Train parallel Medusa heads on the frozen backbone with an auxiliary loss; use tree attention and typical acceptance during decoding.
experiments: Vicuna-7B/13B/33B on MT-Bench and GSM8K, compared against speculative decoding and self-speculative baselines.
results: 2.2x speedup on Vicuna-7B/33B and 2.3x on MT-Bench, with quality matching the baseline.
limitations: Needs additional training and head memory; typical-acceptance robustness is not uniform across settings.
futureDirections: More heads, integration with serving stacks, and extension to other model families.
insights: A guided multi-token predictor trained on the same model can beat generic external draft models.
relevance: Shows how a model-specific accelerator can change token distributions; such output shifts need auditing across demographic groups.

title: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty
abstract: EAGLE drafts autoregressively in the feature (hidden-state) space rather than token space, conditioning on the target model's feature distribution to lower uncertainty and raise acceptance, achieving 2-3x and up to 5x latency reduction.
oneLiner: Draft in the hidden-feature space instead of token space to make draft predictions far more accurate.
keyFinding: Feature-level drafting sharply raises acceptance rates, giving roughly 2-3x latency reduction and up to 5x in some settings while strictly preserving the output distribution.
weakness: The draft header must be retrained for a specific base model, and it adds memory and complexity.
implication: The space in which you draft (features versus tokens) is a dominant factor in speculative decoding efficiency.
contributions: Feature-level autoregressive drafting and a two-stage training scheme for the draft header.
methods: A draft header recursively predicts next-token features that the target model verifies; trained with contrastive/self-distillation objectives.
experiments: Evaluated across Llama2-7B/13B/70B and Vicuna, measuring speedup and acceptance rates against strong baselines.
results: 2-3x speedup on average and up to 5x across model sizes, matching or beating the strongest prior methods.
limitations: Requires model-specific draft-header training; additional memory overhead; gains are model-dependent.
futureDirections: Adaptive acceptance thresholds, cross-architecture generalization, and combination with quantization.
insights: Draft accuracy is the lever for speculative decoding, and feature-space drafting is an effective way to get it.
relevance: Highlights that this acceleration family's ceiling is draft precision, which matters when auditing whether acceleration changes output behavior.

title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
abstract: GPTQ is a one-shot weight quantization method based on approximate second-order information that compresses LLM weights to 3-4 bits while preserving accuracy, enabling accurate and efficient inference on a single GPU.
oneLiner: Compress LLM weights to 3-4 bits with a Hessian-based method that keeps accuracy nearly intact.
keyFinding: GPTQ compresses LLMs to 3-4 bits per weight with only a small perplexity increase and gives 2-3x faster inference.
weakness: The approximate second-order computation is costly upfront; it is weight-only (activations stay high precision); results depend on calibration data.
implication: Post-training quantization can be near-lossless for LLMs without any full retraining.
contributions: A layer-wise quantization algorithm using approximate second-order information, plus a fast batched inverse-Hessian formulation.
methods: Hessian-based (OBQ-style) layer-wise quantization with an efficient batched inverse-Hessian approximation and group-size scaling.
experiments: Quantized OPT and BabelGPT models at 3-4 bits, measuring perplexity and memory versus unquantized baselines.
results: 3-4 bit compression with minimal perplexity change and 2-3x inference speedup.
limitations: Weight-only; needs calibration data; quantization error depends on calibration quality.
futureDirections: Combining with activation-aware methods, refining very-low-bit regimes, and hardware co-design.
insights: Second-order-aware quantization is highly effective, showing model-specific structure can be exploited for compression.
relevance: Low-bit weight compression can interact unequally with the layers an early-exit system keeps, making per-group accuracy auditing relevant.

title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
abstract: AWQ identifies a small set of salient weight channels by observing activation magnitudes rather than weight magnitudes, then protects those channels during quantization, yielding better low-bit quality and enabling on-device LLM serving.
oneLiner: Guard a few important weight channels, found by activation magnitude, to get high-quality low-bit quantization.
keyFinding: AWQ quantizes to 4-bit with much better accuracy than prior methods and enables on-device Llama serving with 3x+ speedups and large memory savings.
weakness: Requires validation-set activation statistics; saliency is per-model; finding salient channels has overhead.
implication: Activation statistics, not raw weight magnitudes, determine which weights need protecting in quantization.
contributions: Activation-aware saliency detection, per-channel scaling, and a hardware-friendly kernel stack for device-side inference.
methods: Detect salient channels from activation magnitude; scale them before quantization; supports group-wise and per-channel quantization.
experiments: Quantized Llama-family and other LLMs; evaluated on perplexity, downstream tasks, and on-device mobile inference.
results: 4-bit quantization with strong accuracy; enables 3x-faster, memory-efficient on-device model serving.
limitations: Requires calibration activations; accuracy degrades at very low bit-widths; saliency detection is heuristic.
futureDirections: Better saliency measures, joint weight-activation quantization, and stronger hardware kernels.
insights: Activation-driven protection of salient weights is a central design principle for low-bit LLM quantization.
relevance: Shows quantization choices are activation-driven; analogous activation-based checks matter for fairness auditing of early-exit systems.

title: SparseGPT: Massive Language Models Can Be Accurately Pruned in One-Shot
abstract: SparseGPT prunes massive LLMs to 50-60% sparsity in a single shot using a scalable layer-wise method that reformulates pruning as sparse regression, removing weights with almost no accuracy loss and no retraining.
oneLiner: Prune giant LLMs down to half their weights in one shot using a scalable sparse-regression method.
keyFinding: SparseGPT removes 50-60% of weights from models up to 175B parameters in one shot with near-zero accuracy loss, without retraining.
weakness: Produces mostly unstructured sparsity that needs specialized hardware to turn into speed; Hessian cost is high; accuracy drops at very high sparsity.
implication: Post-training pruning can yield large weight reduction without retraining, but real speed requires hardware support.
contributions: A scalable one-shot pruning method, a sparse-regression solver, and an efficient GPU implementation.
methods: Layer-wise pruning cast as sparse regression with per-layer updated Hessian reconstruction and row-wise weight selection.
experiments: Pruned OPT models up to 175B to 50-60% sparsity, measuring perplexity and zero-shot accuracy.
results: 50-60% sparsity with minimal perplexity and accuracy loss across multiple LLM scales.
limitations: Unstructured pruning gives limited real speedup without sparsity-aware hardware; needs the full model in memory.
futureDirections: Structured sparsity variants, combining with quantization, and hardware co-design.
insights: LLMs are highly compressible through pruning, but realized speedups depend on structured or hardware support.
relevance: Pruning changes which weights survive; the resulting output differences across demographic groups could be audited for fairness.

title: LLM-Pruner: On the Structural Pruning of Large Language Models
abstract: LLM-Pruner performs structural pruning of LLMs by removing coupled structures (attention heads, FFN channels) selected by gradient-based importance in a task-agnostic way, then lightly fine-tunes to recover performance.
oneLiner: Prune whole structures such as heads and channels using gradient importance, then recover with light fine-tuning.
keyFinding: Structural pruning reduces LLaMA-7B to roughly 2.7B-equivalent FLOPs with only modest loss in zero-shot accuracy.
weakness: Requires a fine-tuning stage to recover accuracy, and instruction-following ability degrades; quality loss is not fully zero.
implication: Real hardware speed and memory gains require structural (not just unstructured) pruning, which costs some accuracy.
contributions: Task-agnostic structural pruning via gradient saliency on coupled structures, plus a light post-pruning tuning recipe.
methods: Gradient-based importance scoring; prune grouped/connected structures (heads, FFN channels); short fine-tuning to recover.
experiments: Pruned LLaMA-7B and Vicuna; evaluated on zero-shot and instruction tasks, measuring FLOPs and memory.
results: Roughly 2.7B-equivalent FLOPs reduction with slight zero-shot degradation and modest memory savings.
limitations: Needs fine-tuning; sensitive to the tuning budget; instruction following degrades.
futureDirections: Better importance metrics, task-specific pruning, and combinations with quantization.
insights: Structural pruning is the practical path to real speedups but requires recovery training.
relevance: Removing attention heads or depth layers changes which language patterns are preserved, directly relevant to fairness auditing.

title: H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models
abstract: H2O introduces an attention KV-cache eviction policy that keeps a small set of frequently-attended 'heavy-hitter' tokens plus recent tokens, reducing cache memory by up to 20x and improving throughput while maintaining quality.
oneLiner: Keep only the frequently-attended 'heavy-hitter' tokens plus recent ones to shrink the KV cache dramatically.
keyFinding: H2O cuts KV-cache memory by up to 20x and boosts throughput while keeping or improving generation quality over baselines.
weakness: Uses a heuristic importance measure; may drop tokens critical for long-context reasoning, so quality can degrade on some tasks.
implication: Not all past tokens matter equally; attention-based selection can greatly reduce memory without much accuracy loss.
contributions: An attention-guided KV-cache eviction framework and the heavy-hitter oracle for dynamic cache allocation.
methods: Track accumulated attention per token; retain top heavy hitters plus a sliding window; update cache dynamically.
experiments: Evaluated on multiple LLMs and long-context datasets, measuring memory, throughput, and quality.
results: Up to 20x cache reduction and higher throughput while preserving quality.
limitations: Heuristic importance; relies on attention as oracle; risk to long-context accuracy.
futureDirections: Learning-based eviction, stronger importance measures, and serving-system integration.
insights: Attention statistics are a strong prior for which keys matter, an idea central to cache compression.
relevance: KV eviction decides which context is remembered; which tokens get dropped could differ across demographic groups.

title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
abstract: StreamingLLM observes that streaming LLMs need 'attention sinks' (a few initial tokens) to stabilize attention, and combines them with a rolling window to enable stable inference over millions of tokens with constant, efficient memory and no recomputation.
oneLiner: Keep a few initial 'sink' tokens in the KV cache so attention stays stable over millions of generated tokens.
keyFinding: Attention sinks plus a local sliding window let LLMs stream over more than 4M tokens with constant memory and no quality collapse.
weakness: Performance depends on sink curation; it is not full model understanding; benefits apply mainly to very long streaming contexts.
implication: KV-cache memory can be made constant even for unbounded generation by retaining a minimal set of sink tokens.
contributions: Analysis of the attention-sink phenomenon and a streaming-inference method with a fixed cache and local window.
methods: Keep a few initial sink tokens plus a sliding window of recent tokens, avoiding recomputation of the full history.
experiments: Tested on Llama-2, MPT, and Pythia; evaluated on streaming tasks and sequences longer than 4M tokens.
results: Stable streaming beyond 4M tokens with constant memory and efficient throughput.
limitations: Sink initialization matters; limited to streaming generation; quality not uniform across all tasks.
futureDirections: Better sink selection, combining with cache compression, and training-aware sink design.
insights: Attention needs a small persistent anchor set, which is a subtle cue for cache-management design.
relevance: Shows that the attention module's behavior can be strongly shaped by a few retained tokens, relevant to how context is parametrized and audited.

title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
abstract: FlashAttention is an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that computes attention in tiles without materializing the large intermediate attention matrix, using recomputation to cut memory and improve wall-clock speed.
oneLiner: Compute exact attention in tiles, never writing the full attention matrix to HBM, so it is faster and far more memory-efficient.
keyFinding: FlashAttention delivers 2-4x wall-clock speedup and large memory savings, enabling much longer sequence lengths, and later versions scale attention to even more hardware.
weakness: Optimized for GPU HBM/BF16; gains are hardware-specific; it is an implementation improvement, not a change to the attention math.
implication: A large part of achievable attention speedup is an I/O and memory-efficiency problem rather than an algorithmic one.
contributions: Tiled exact attention with no intermediate materialization plus IO-aware analysis and fused kernels; refined in FlashAttention-2.
methods: Compute softmax in blocks (tiling), use online softmax, and recompute to avoid storing the full attention matrix; fused CUDA kernels.
experiments: Benchmarked on GPT-2-style models and others; measured speed and memory on A100, enabling longer-context training.
results: 2-4x speedup and substantial memory reduction, enabling much larger sequence lengths.
limitations: Hardware-specific to GPUs; produces the exact same attention; benefits are implementation-level.
futureDirections: Extending to more hardware, longer contexts, and integration with other attention variants.
insights: IO-aware kernel design is a major, largely orthogonal source of LLM speedups.
relevance: Attention-serving efficiency is the baseline every early-exit and dynamic-depth method is compared against.

title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models
abstract: Mixture-of-Depths introduces a router that dynamically selects which tokens pass through each transformer block, letting tokens skip computation while preserving the model's FLOPs budget and overall capacity.
oneLiner: Let a router decide per token which layers to skip, so compute is allocated only where it is needed.
keyFinding: MoD matches baseline quality while using about half the FLOPs per forward pass and matching the latency of a much smaller model through dynamic token routing.
weakness: Requires training-time routing; router quality tradeoffs; and hard to exploit without adaptive runtime or hardware support.
implication: Token-level dynamic depth lets a model spend compute proportional to token difficulty, a foundational idea for early exit.
contributions: Router-based token-to-depth assignment, auxiliary balancing losses, and a wait-for-completion mechanism to prevent latency spikes.
methods: Router on hidden states; top-k token selection per block; auxiliary balance loss; token-dropping behavior at inference.
experiments: Trained decoder-only transformers across several scales, measuring loss, FLOPs, and inference latency.
results: Comparable quality at roughly 50% FLOPs with the latency of a smaller model.
limitations: Needs specialized training; routing can drop important tokens; deployment needs adaptive scheduling.
futureDirections: Inference-time dynamic depth, better routers, and hardware co-design.
insights: Skip decisions can be made per token at training time, reducing compute while preserving model capacity.
relevance: This is the closest analog to early-exit dynamic depth; routing fairness across tokens and groups is directly relevant to the research topic.

title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
abstract: The paper shows that many of the deepest layers of trained LLMs contribute negligibly at inference, and that dropping them with a cheap layer-selection heuristic preserves performance while enabling faster inference, with some tasks even improving.
oneLiner: Many of an LLM's deepest layers hardly matter, so you can drop them at inference for a nearly-free speedup.
keyFinding: Dropping roughly half of the deepest layers of a 70B model gives about 1.5x speedup on a consumer GPU with minimal performance loss; some tasks like MMLU even improve.
weakness: Performance is task-dependent; dropping layers can hurt reasoning and math; the simple heuristic selection is not always optimal.
implication: Depth-wise redundancy can be exploited for inference-time early exit at nearly zero cost.
contributions: A layer-selection and layer-pruning method with an analysis of layer contribution, plus a benchmark across tasks.
methods: Select deeper layers of the forward pass to drop (using a proxy measure) and evaluate quality against retained depth.
experiments: Tested on Llama-2 and Llama-3 up to 70B; measured quality across tasks and speedup on consumer hardware.
results: About 1.5x speedup from dropping roughly 50% of layers with minimal loss, and MMLU can improve.
limitations: Task-dependent losses; no rigorous per-task optimal policy; heuristic layer selection.
futureDirections: Better or learned layer-drop policies, per-request dynamic depth, and combining with quantization.
insights: Layer redundancy supports cheap inference-time depth control, a direct precedent for early exit.
relevance: Directly relevant to early exit: deciding which layers to drop determines the output changes that must be audited for demographic fairness.
